subject: Sanitization policy options and residency/retention for PHI - Q&A

Subject: Data residency/retention and redaction options for PHI - quick questions

Hi Ben,

Thanks for the demo last week. We have a follow-up from our security and compliance team: two quick, high-level questions to help us scope an internal decision.

1) Retention limits: for PHI-derived outputs (summaries, annotations) what typical retention windows do you recommend for regulated healthcare customers? We need a short list (e.g., 30/90/365 days) that maps to tradeoffs you see in cost and operational complexity.

2) Redaction/sanitization options: we want to understand realistic approaches you support for removing or obfuscating PHI at ingest and at rest. Specifically: field-level permanent redaction, reversible tokenization, pseudonymization, and whether redaction can be applied retroactively to cached request/response artifacts.

Also: what logs/audit evidence can you provide to satisfy an external audit request (timestamped deletion events, exportable audit logs, and proof of KV-cache flushes)?

Appreciate concise answers we can pass to our legal/compliance folks. If it helps, we can schedule 30 min with Rishi and your security engineer.

Best,
Sarah
Director, Security Compliance
Harbor Healthcare

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Data residency/retention and redaction options for PHI - quick questions

Hi Sarah — great questions. Below is a pragmatic breakdown you can share with legal/compliance. I kept it concise and highlighted tradeoffs. Attaching a short playbook (redwood-sanitization-options-v1.pdf) and an example audit export.

Retention (recommended default tiers)
- 30 days: lowest cost + simplest (good for ephemeral chat/triage). Minimal log retention, fast KV-cache eviction.
- 90 days: common compromise for non-longitudinal PHI artifacts (summaries, annotations). Allows short-term troubleshooting and A/B quality checks.
- 365 days: used when business/legal requires year-long traces (billing disputes, clinical continuity). Higher storage and audit complexity.
Tradeoffs: shorter windows reduce storage and retention of cached embeddings; longer windows increase cost and require stronger key management and rotation policies.

Sanitization / Redaction options we support
1) Pre-ingest field-level redaction: non-reversible removal of named fields before any tokenization or embedding. Strongest guarantee if done client-side or at gateway.
2) Server-side deterministic pseudonymization: replace identifiers with consistent pseudonyms (useful when you need linkage but not original value). Reversibility depends on where the mapping store lives — we recommend customer-managed KMS + mapping store for reversible mapping.
3) Tokenization (reversible): we can integrate with customer token vaults (customer-managed) for reversible tokens; requires contractual controls if reversible.
4) Post-ingest scrub + reingest: we support a scrub pipeline that can retroactively remove fields and then re-ingest sanitized artifacts — works for stored artifacts but not for in-memory KV cache unless cache flush is triggered (see below).

Cache/Runtime considerations
- KV cache: we provide an API to invalidate/flush per-tenant caches. Flushing is immediate for active processes but you should plan a short rollback window if you rely on prefix caching for latency.
- Embeddings and derived artifacts: if embeddings were persisted externally (DB or vector store) we provide scripts and tooling to locate and remove vectors by metadata tag. Note that embeddings derived from sensitive text are irreversible; redaction removes the original text but cannot 'ungenerate' vectors already used by downstream stores without explicit deletion.

Auditability / Evidence for audits
- Exportable audit logs: timestamped events (object created, deleted, redaction applied, cache flush) with request IDs. Provided as CSV/JSON exports.
- Deletion proof: we can provide signed deletion events (hash+timestamp) for storage objects.
- Access logs: token-level access trails available via Console with retention window matching your plan.

Next steps: I copied Marissa to coordinate Contract/SOW needs and Rishi (our security lead) to chime in on the KMS/mapping specifics. Would you like 30 minutes tomorrow or Friday for a quick walkthrough?

Regards,

Subject: Re: Data residency/retention and redaction options for PHI - quick questions

Hi Sarah — Rishi from Security. A few technical clarifications to help your controls team evaluate risk: 

1) Strongest guarantees: pre-ingest client-side redaction or gateway-level transformation (never leave original data on disk) is the most robust for regulated PHI. If you must preserve originals, keep mapping tokens in customer-owned stores (VPC-hosted DB) with strict KMS access.

2) Retroactive removal: we can delete objects and issue signed deletion receipts. For runtime artifacts:
   - KV cache: we support tenant-scoped eviction calls (immediate). We persist cache-invalidation events to audit logs.
   - Worker / GPU memory: clearing memory is immediate but cannot be retroactively validated after process termination; rely on deletion receipts for persisted artifacts.

3) Embeddings: treat them as primary artifacts — if you need them removed, we will run metadata-tag based deletion across vector stores and provide a deletion report. Note: if third-party vector stores exist outside the Redwood environment, deletion will require coordination.

4) Proof for auditors: we provide
   - Signed deletion receipts (SHA256 digest + timestamp + signer id)
   - Exportable audit logs with event types and correlation IDs
   - Evidence of KMS rotations and CMK metadata (when customer-managed KMS is used)

5) Operational playbook we recommend for regulated workflows:
   - Define retention tier per artifact class (raw transcript, summary, annotations, embeddings)
   - Enforce client-side redaction for raw identifiers where possible
   - Use pseudonymization for analytics cohorts where linkage is needed
   - Schedule regular deletion jobs and capture signed receipts
   - Monitor cache eviction and record events in the audit stream

I can walk your engineers through the KMS integration and the deletion API. If Harbor needs us to run a one-off scrub to bring an existing dataset into compliance, we will propose a timeboxed engagement with a deletion report.

—Rishi Malhotra
